Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers «Directive (EU) 2023/959 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 amending Directive 2003/87/EC establishing a system for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Union and Decision (EU) 2015/1814» It is an EU directive; it applies in the European Union through national law, and it was adopted as stated: «Done at Strasbourg, 10 May 2023.»

Statements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission report of 31 December 2026 set out in section 6.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

This Directive revises the EU Emissions Trading System: it adds maritime transport, tightens the cap and creates a second system for buildings and road transport fuels. The effective date: «The new rules entered into force on 5 June 2023.»

It is addressed to Member States, so it applies as national law once transposed: «Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with Article 1 of this Directive by 31 December 2023. They shall apply those measures from 1 January 2024.» «However, Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with the following articles by 30 June 2024»

For a freight forwarder it matters on ocean legs touching EU ports and, from the second system, on the fuels released for consumption that it covers; the source does not state how either cost reaches a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the Directive is addressed to the Member States and names no duty on a forwarder. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The first maritime surrender date has passed: «Shipping companies must surrender (use) their first ETS allowances by 30 September 2025 for emissions reported in 2024.» Later surrender dates follow the same annual rule.

*Operational implication:* an ocean pricing lead records, before the next quote run, whether each shipping company states an allowance charge, with the allowance price and date it states.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty holders are Member States for transposition, shipping companies for ocean legs, and, in the new second system, regulated entities that release fuels for consumption pursuant to Annex III. «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 31 May each year, the regulated entity surrenders an amount of allowances covered by this Chapter that is equal to the regulated entity’s total emissions, corresponding to the quantity of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III, during the preceding calendar year»

The text requires a report on how much of that cost is passed on: «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year until 2030, each regulated entity reports the average share of costs related to the surrender of allowances under this Chapter which it passed on to consumers for the preceding year.»

A freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys fuel for its own trucks falls within the regulated entity concept is not stated in these passages and should be confirmed with counsel; the source does not state how the cost reaches a forwarder that buys road legs.

## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

The Commission's questions and answers on maritime transport, cited as guidance and not as the Directive, state the ship types in scope: «Since 2024: cargo and passenger ships of or above 5000 gross tonnage (GT) From 2027: offshore ships of or above 5000 GT»

*Industry interpretation:* the answers are the Commission's reading of the Directive and are not part of the legal text.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

Dated Commission steps: «No later than 31 December 2026, the Commission shall present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council in which it shall examine the feasibility and economic, environmental and social impacts of the inclusion in this Directive of emissions from ships, including offshore ships, below 5 000 gross tonnage but not below 400 gross tonnage» The report due by 31 July 2026 has passed, and the sources do not show whether it was published: «By 31 July 2026, the Commission shall report to the European Parliament and to the Council on the following matters»

The scope widens on dated days: «From 1 January 2026 and 1 January 2027 respectively, the quantity of allowances shall be increased to take into account the coverage of greenhouse gas emissions other than CO 2 emissions from maritime transport activities and the coverage of emissions of offshore ships» The 1 January 2026 step has passed; the 1 January 2027 offshore step is ahead.

*Analytical inference:* the report on smaller ships examines their inclusion and the offshore step increases the quantity of allowances for offshore ships; the sources do not say what the Commission will propose.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

The new substantive requirements are a second allowance system for building and road transport fuels, a phase-in for ships, and a lower cap.

- Second system monitoring and reporting: «Member States shall ensure that each regulated entity monitors for each calendar year from 2025 the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III. They shall also ensure that each regulated entity reports those emissions to the competent authority in the following year, starting in 2026»
- Second system surrender: see section 4, «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 31 May each year, the regulated entity surrenders an amount of allowances covered by this Chapter that is equal to the regulated entity’s total emissions, corresponding to the quantity of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III, during the preceding calendar year»
- Price stability in the second system, until 31 December 2029: «Where the average price of allowances referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article exceeds a price of EUR 45 for a period of two consecutive months, 20 million allowances covered by this Chapter shall be released from the market stability reserve» «Allowances shall be released through the mechanism provided for in this paragraph up to 31 December 2029.»
- National tax derogation: «Until 31 December 2030, by way of derogation from paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, where a regulated entity established in a given Member State is subject to a national carbon tax in force for the years 2027 to 2030»
- Cap path: «The linear factor shall be 4,3 % from 2024 to 2027 and 4,4 % from 2028.»
- Maritime phase-in: «(a) 40 % of verified emissions reported for 2024 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (b) 70 % of verified emissions reported for 2025 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (c) 100 % of verified emissions reported for 2026 and each year thereafter»
- Border adjustment: «From 2034, no CBAM factor shall apply.»
- Permit: «Member States shall ensure that, from 1 January 2025, no regulated entity carries out the activity referred to in Annex III unless that regulated entity holds a permit issued by a competent authority»
- Scope of the second system: «the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III»

*Analytical inference:* the second system attaches a surrender duty to the fuels released for consumption under Annex III from the 2028 surrender start, and 20 million allowances are released from the market stability reserve when the average price exceeds EUR 45 for two consecutive months; the text does not state a fuel price effect.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the second-system monitoring, reporting, permit and surrender duties fall on the regulated entity that releases fuels for consumption under Annex III; whether a forwarder that buys fuel for its own trucks is a regulated entity, and whether the national carbon tax derogation applies in a given Member State, are questions for counsel.

No phase-in is stated outside the dated steps above. No exceptions are stated in Article 5. No scope limits are stated in Article 5 beyond the entry into force.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The reporting duties sit with regulated entities, shipping companies and Member States: «Member States shall ensure that each regulated entity monitors for each calendar year from 2025 the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III. They shall also ensure that each regulated entity reports those emissions to the competent authority in the following year, starting in 2026» «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year until 2030, each regulated entity reports the average share of costs related to the surrender of allowances under this Chapter which it passed on to consumers for the preceding year.»

The penalty summary is a gap in this item: the captured text of the amending Directive states no penalty amount. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the text sets no registration or reporting duty for a freight forwarder.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a quote field and a contract question.

- A road pricing lead records, at the next quote run, whether each carrier states a carbon cost component in its fuel cost, and the basis it states.
- An ocean procurement lead asks each shipping company in the next contract round how it recovers allowance cost.

*Operational implication:* both steps use only the provisions quoted and no allowance price.

## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 10 May 2023: the Directive is adopted at Strasbourg
- 5 June 2023: the new rules enter into force
- 31 December 2023: transposition deadline for Article 1
- 1 January 2024: Member States apply the measures
- 30 June 2024: transposition deadline for the buildings and road transport provisions
- 30 September 2025: first maritime surrender date, for emissions reported in 2024
- 1 January 2025: a permit is required for regulated entities in the second system
- 2025: monitoring of fuel emissions begins in the second system
- 1 January 2026: quantity of allowances increases for non-CO2 gases from ships
- 31 July 2026: Commission reports (date passed)
- 31 December 2026: Commission report on smaller ships
- 1 January 2027: quantity of allowances increases for offshore ships
- 1 January 2028: second system surrender begins
- 31 December 2030: national carbon tax derogation ends
- 2034: no CBAM factor applies

This document covers an EU regulation that amends the CO2 standards for new heavy-duty vehicles and applies in the European Union. «Article 1

Amendments to Regulation (EU) 2019/1242

Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 is amended as follows» «This Regulation sets CO 2 emissions performance standards for new heavy-duty vehicles. Those standards contribute to achieving the Union’s climate-neutrality objective and the intermediate Union climate targets»

It was adopted at «Done at Brussels, 14 May 2024.» *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission review of the amended Regulation set out in section 6. Statements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulation tightens the CO2 targets that truck and bus manufacturers have to meet for new vehicles. The effective date is stated in Article 5: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .
It shall apply from 1 July 2024.» «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.»

*Analytical inference:* for a freight forwarder that buys road legs, the targets set the fleet average reduction for new heavy-duty vehicles (claim 7), the vehicles road carriers operate; the source states no effect on carriers, truck supply or price. The text states that the targets are complemented by charging and refuelling rules: «The Union fleet-wide CO 2 emissions reduction targets laid down in this Regulation are complemented by the recharging and refuelling infrastructure requirements set out in Regulation (EU) 2023/1804»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the targets are addressed to manufacturers; no duty on a freight forwarder is stated, and the source states no effect on carriers or forwarders. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step that touches a forwarder is a Commission report on fleet operators in mid-2027. «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which contains an analysis of the potential need for and impact of initiatives to increase the share of zero-emission heavy-duty motor vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators.»

*Operational implication:* a regulatory lead for a forwarder that owns or leases heavy trucks prepares a short fleet profile (number of heavy-duty vehicles, share electric) in the coming quarter, so that the forwarder can respond to the report; the decision that changes on 30 June 2027 is how to respond to the Commission's analysis of the need for initiatives on the zero-emission share of vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators; the text does not say what the analysis will find.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty holders are manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles, measured as a Union fleet average. «The average CO 2 emissions of the Union fleet of new heavy-duty motor vehicles, other than special purpose vehicles, off-road vehicles and off-road special purpose vehicles shall be reduced by the following percentages compared to the average CO 2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019»

A freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys heavy trucks for its own fleet takes any role under the Regulation is not stated; the source states no effect on a forwarder that buys road legs.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The Regulation sets several Commission reports. Two have passed their dates, the report due on 30 June 2025 and the report due on 31 December 2025: «By 30 June 2025, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which considers the need to facilitate the uptake on the Union market of heavy-duty vehicles which are retrofitted to become zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles, including by way of harmonised rules.» «the Commission shall by 31 December 2025 present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council with a comprehensive analysis of the need to further incentivise the uptake of advanced biofuels and biogas and renewable fuels of non-biological origin» The review that remains ahead is: «By 31 December 2027, the Commission shall review the effectiveness and impact of this Regulation, in particular as regards the objective of climate neutrality at the latest by 2050»

The 30 June 2027 report on large fleet operators is set out in section 3. *Analytical inference:* the review is the next dated assessment of the Regulation; the text does not say whether it will change the 2030, 2035 or 2040 steps. The captured pages do not say whether the 2025 reports were published.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

The substantive requirement is a stepped reduction of manufacturer fleet CO2 against the 2019 reporting period.

- «15 % for vehicle sub-groups 4-UD, 4-RD, 4-LH, 5-RD, 5-LH, 9-RD, 9-LH, 10-RD and 10-LH for the reporting periods of the years 2025 to 2029;»
- «45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034;»
- «65 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the years 2035 to 2039;»
- «90 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the year 2040 onwards.»
- Urban buses: «manufacturers shall comply with the 90 % and 100 % minimum shares of zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles in their fleet of new heavy-duty vehicles»
- Data penalty: «The administrative fines shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and shall not exceed EUR 30 000 for each heavy-duty vehicle concerned by deviating or delayed data»
- Exception for some approved vehicles: «approved heavy-duty vehicles falling under Article 2(3), first subparagraph, point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 shall not be subject to the CO 2 emissions reduction targets»

*Analytical inference:* the percentages step up at 2030, 2035 and 2040, so the fleet average CO2 reduction a manufacturer must reach rises in three steps; the captured text states the percentages and not the vehicle mix that meets them.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the fleet reduction targets, the urban bus zero-emission shares and the administrative fines bind manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles; whether a forwarder that has vehicles built or converted for its own fleet is treated as a manufacturer, and whether a given vehicle falls under the Article 2(3) exception, are questions for counsel.

No phase-in is stated in Articles 1 and 5 beyond the dates above. No exceptions are stated in Article 3a. No scope limits are stated in Article 5 other than the entry into force.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The text sets no reporting duty for a forwarder; the provision quoted is the Commission's power to fine a manufacturer over reported data: «The Commission may impose an administrative fine in each of the following cases»

The penalty summary is therefore limited: the fine cap in section 8 is the only amount stated, and the premium on excess CO2 emissions is a gap in the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the rules on the excess emissions premium are outside the captured text.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a procurement field, not a system change.

- A procurement lead adds, at the next carrier onboarding round, to the road carrier onboarding form a field for the share of zero-emission vehicles in the carrier's heavy-duty fleet and the year its fleet plan assumes, so that the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps can be read against it.

*Operational implication:* this step uses only the dates the text states and no cost figure.

## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 14 May 2024: the Regulation is adopted at Brussels
- 1 July 2024: the Regulation begins to apply
- 2025: first reporting-period step, with a 15 % reduction for listed sub-groups
- 31 December 2025: Commission report on renewable fuels in heavy-duty vehicles
- 30 June 2027: Commission report on large fleet operators
- 31 December 2027: Commission review of the Regulation
- 2030: 45 % reduction step
- 2035: 65 % reduction step
- 2040: 90 % reduction step
- 2050: climate neutrality objective at the latest

What the Research Found

The finding is a University of Cambridge Department of Engineering and Centre for Sustainable Road Freight consortium research programme on UK electric heavy goods vehicles: «The trial will pool operations and technical data from a fleet of rigid and articulated eHGVs being used across a wide range of 3PL, retailer and manufacturer use cases.» Under the programme, a participating retailer operates an electric tractor unit in its UK logistics operation: «The vehicle, a Volvo FM 4x2 tractor unit, is a heavy-duty truck that can carry up to 42 tonnes and can cover up to 300km on a single charge.»

The methodology limits are the shared-trial structure and confidentiality scope before results are published: «High resolution operational data will be collected during each trial period and then analysed, anonymised, and shared with all partners as part of a managed collective learning process. All shared data will be subject to the provisions of a Data Confidentiality Agreement which will be agreed between all partners before the work starts.»

*Analytical inference:* pooling data across partner trials under a confidentiality agreement builds shared models for participating operators, but the launch announcement itself publishes no route-level energy consumption or cost dataset.

## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

This matters operationally and commercially because the consortium is structured to inform fleet and charger investment decisions: «The objective is to develop the knowledge and models needed to de-risk electric freight operations and inform investment decisions. The participating fleet operators will share their learning experiences in a pre-competitive environment to develop a clear understanding of how electric vehicles and charging infrastructure can be deployed most effectively to serve their business needs.» Academic researchers in the consortium model both operational and cost performance: «Specialists at Cambridge University and Heriot-Watt University will analyse and model data including vehicle and charger performance, operational efficiency, and costs across as many industry uses as possible.»

*Industry interpretation:* the university release states the modelling scope and the 42 tonnes and 300km vehicle specification, but gives no trial cost outputs or tariff figures, so it is a research programme baseline rather than a cost fact.

## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

What the finding changes is the evidence structure available to participating UK road operators: shared access to electric trucks, mobile chargers and university modelling across logistics, retail and manufacturing use cases. As of the 2024 programme announcement («© 2024 Project JOLT All rights reserved»), whole-fleet transition feasibility was still open and no post-trial dataset is held: «Operators are purchasing and running these vehicles today in fleets of all sizes. But there’s still a long way to go to understand how whole fleets and industries can transition to electric heavy goods vehicles in a technically feasible way.»

*Operational implication:* a procurement lead for UK road legs, when a road carrier cites electric heavy goods vehicle capability on a lane in the next tender, asks which vehicle payload up to 42 tonnes, single-charge range up to 300km and charging setup the carrier has run.

## 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

What the finding does not resolve, as of the 2024 programme announcement (no later post-trial dataset is held), is whole-fleet transition feasibility, charger downtime effects or modelled cost figures across duty cycles. The source authority signal is the academic-industry research collaboration leading the trial: «SRF was founded to help industry and government minimise carbon emissions from the road freight sector and is a collaboration between Cambridge University, Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, the University of Westminster, and industry and government partners.» The evidence agreement signal is not stated beyond the university and partner launch statements, and the release publishes no empirical trial results or cost figures.

Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 on CO2 emission performance standards for new heavy-duty vehicles, as it stands after the 2024 amendment, and applies in the European Union. «this Regulation sets CO 2 emission performance requirements for new heavy-duty vehicles whereby the specific CO 2 emissions of the Union fleet of new heavy-duty vehicles shall be reduced compared to the reference CO 2 emissions as follows: (a) for the reporting periods of the year 2025 onwards by 15 %» The 2019 text appeared as «L_2019198EN.01020201.xml 25.7.2019» in the Official Journal on 25 July 2019, and the amending act was adopted as stated: «Done at Brussels, 14 May 2024.»

Statements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where a freight forwarder's role is not named in the text. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission review set out in section 6; the 15 % figure quoted above is the original text for the reporting periods from 2025; the later steps in section 8 come from the 2024 amendment.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulation sets the fleet CO2 standard that truck manufacturers have to meet for new heavy-duty vehicles. «Article 2 Scope 1. This Regulation shall apply to new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3 that meet the following characteristics» The effective date of the amended provisions of this Regulation is stated in the amending act: «It shall apply from 1 July 2024.»

For a freight forwarder that buys road legs, *Analytical inference:* the standards bind manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3 (claim 3), the vehicles road carriers operate; the source states no effect on carriers, truck supply or prices. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the standards are addressed to manufacturers; no duty on a freight forwarder is stated, and the source states no effect on carriers or forwarders. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step that touches a forwarder is the fleet operator report in mid-2027. «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which contains an analysis of the potential need for and impact of initiatives to increase the share of zero-emission heavy-duty motor vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators.»

*Operational implication:* a regulatory lead for a forwarder that owns or leases heavy trucks prepares a short fleet profile in the coming quarter; the decision that changes on 30 June 2027 is how to respond to the Commission's analysis of the need for initiatives on the zero-emission share of vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators; the text does not say what the analysis will find.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty holders in the text are manufacturers, Member States and the Commission. «Starting from 1 July 2020, and in each subsequent reporting period, the Commission shall determine for each manufacturer the average specific CO 2 emissions in g/tkm for the preceding reporting period»

A freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys heavy trucks for its own fleet takes any role under the Regulation is not stated; the source states no effect on a forwarder that buys road legs.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

One dated review of this Regulation bears on heavy-duty road freight: «By 31 December 2027, the Commission shall review the effectiveness and impact of this Regulation, in particular as regards the objective of climate neutrality at the latest by 2050»

*Analytical inference:* the review assesses the effectiveness and impact of the Regulation; the text does not say whether it will change the 2030, 2035 or 2040 steps.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

The substantive requirement is a manufacturer fleet standard, with a premium for missing it.

- Baseline: «shall be reduced by the following percentages compared to the average CO 2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019»
- «45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034;»
- «65 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the years 2035 to 2039;»
- «90 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the year 2040 onwards.»
- Premium: «Where a manufacturer is found, pursuant to paragraph 2, to have excess CO 2 emissions in a given reporting period from 2025 onwards, the Commission shall impose an excess CO 2 emissions premium, calculated in accordance with the following formula: (a) from 2025 to 2029, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 4 250 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm)»
- «(b) from 2030 onwards, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 6 800 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm)»
- Scope: «Article 2 Scope 1. This Regulation shall apply to new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3»
- Exception: «approved heavy-duty vehicles falling under Article 2(3), first subparagraph, point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 shall not be subject to the CO 2 emissions reduction targets»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the fleet standard, the excess emissions premium and the scope of Article 2 bind manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3; whether a forwarder that has vehicles built or converted for its own fleet is treated as a manufacturer, and whether a given vehicle falls under the Article 2(3) exception, are questions for counsel.

*Analytical inference:* the premium per gram of CO2 per tonne-kilometre rises between 2025 and 2030, so a manufacturer that misses the 2030 step pays a higher rate than a manufacturer that misses the 2025 step by the same amount; the text gives no per-vehicle price effect, so the effect on a truck price is not stated.

No phase-in is stated beyond the reporting-period steps above. No exceptions are stated in Article 3a. Its 2030 step leaves out vocational vehicles, a scope limit.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The reporting duties in the text sit with manufacturers, Member States and the Commission, not with forwarders: «By 30 April each year, the Commission shall, by means of implementing acts, publish a list indicating»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the detail of Member State reporting on registered vehicles is outside the passages quoted here.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a procurement field, not a system change.

- A procurement lead adds, at the next carrier onboarding round, to the road carrier onboarding form a field for the share of zero-emission vehicles in the carrier's heavy-duty fleet and the year its fleet plan assumes, so that the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps can be read against it.

*Operational implication:* this step uses only the dates the text states and no cost figure.

What the Research Found

The finding is that the International Maritime Organization has no adopted global fuel standard or carbon price for shipping as of the assessment update of «26 Mar 2026». «The IMO failed to adopt the Net Zero Framework (NZF), a global fuel standard and carbon pricing mechanism, at the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s (MEPC) extraordinary session in October 2025.» «International shipping accounts for about 2.3% of global CO 2 emissions in 2023 (ICCT, 2025).» «With the current level of policy action, CO 2 emissions are projected to be between 729-768 MtCO 2 in 2030 (based on a voyage-based approach), only representing a 1-6% decrease below the reference emissions level in 2008.»

*Analytical inference:* the assessment is a rating of policy ambition by a tracker, not a regulatory text, and its numbers are projections; they say where emissions go against the 2008 reference level if no new measure is adopted, not what any rule requires.

## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

The finding matters operationally because the global measure that would have set one rule for all ocean carriers was not adopted; the source does not state what applies to carriers in its place. «Instead of abandoning the NZF, governments decided to postpone the vote to October 2026.» The source also names the earlier IMO efficiency measures, the Energy Efficiency of Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), which the source judges as working against near-term ambition: «Instead, the EEXI and CII have a counterproductive impact on near-term ambition: the measures promote a switch to LNG-powered ships, resulting in greater GHG emissions»

*Operational implication:* an ocean forwarder cannot assume a single global carbon cost on bunker fuel from the IMO before the postponed vote; this source names no other pricing basis. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.

## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

The finding changes the planning assumption for ocean carbon cost: a global economic instrument expected from 2027 is not in force and its adoption is open. «Current policies put the shipping sector far off track from achieving the IMO’s target of reducing emissions by 20% and striving for 30% by 2030, with an implementation gap of 109–186 MtCO 2 .» «Agreed to a fuel-based target of at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used in international shipping to come from zero and “near zero” emission fuels and technologies by 2030.»

*Analytical inference:* a freight forwarder that told clients to expect one global measure should state instead that no global measure is adopted and that it depends on a vote the source places in October 2026; the source does not name the cost basis that applies meanwhile.

## 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

What the finding does not resolve: «It is unclear how the postponement will affect the agreed technical measures.» The vote itself is the open item: «postpone the vote to October 2026» The capture does not report the outcome of that vote.

The methodology limits are that the numbers are projections on a voyage-based approach «(based on a voyage-based approach)»; the evidence agreement signal and the source authority signal are not stated in the captured text beyond the publisher name. «an ‘economic instrument’ (i.e. a market-based measure) for adoption in 2025, with implementation expected from 2027» «Agreed to consider long-term measures beyond 2030 as part of the review of the Strategy in 2028.»

- October 2026: member states' postponed vote on the Net Zero Framework
- 2027: implementation of an economic instrument had been expected from 2027
- 2028: review of the Strategy

What's Moving and What Triggered It

The signal event is a sharp rise in global air cargo spot rates during a Middle East shipping disruption. «Global air cargo spot rates rose 41% year-on-year in May to an average of $3.40 per kg, driven by resilient demand, constrained capacity and ongoing geopolitical disruptions, according to Xeneta.» «Long-term contract rates, which increased 22% year-on-year, eased after reaching a peak at the end of April»

The industry body's April figures give the volume side: «increased by 4.0% compared to April 2025 levels (+4.0% for international operations). Capacity, measured in available cargo tonne-kilometers (ACTK), decreased by -0.4% compared to April 2025»

*Analytical inference:* the 41% is a year-on-year comparison of a monthly average from one rate benchmarking provider; it is not a rate for any named lane, and the captured pages give no figure for ocean container rates.

## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want

The driving parties are Tehran, as reported by Tasnim, the carriers whose hubs and routes are disrupted, and the shippers buying capacity. «Iran's state-affiliated outlet Tasnim reported that Tehran was halting negotiations entirely and had resolved to fully close the Strait of Hormuz and “activate other fronts including the Bab al-Mandeb Strait,” a critical shipping lane linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.»

«Severe disruption at major Gulf hubs due to the war in the Middle East continued to reshape trade routes and constrain capacity on key corridors.»

*Industry interpretation:* the Tasnim statement is a report of a statement by a state-affiliated outlet, cited as reported and not as a fact about what Iran has done or will do.

## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers

The conversion trigger is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the return of Gulf carrier capacity: «analysts warn it could take months for normal traffic to resume in the Strait» In its update the rate provider expected relief ahead of that; both windows it named have since passed, and the captured pages do not report whether the easing occurred: «Xeneta believes pricing pressures on shippers may begin to ease in June as capacity returns and demand growth moderates.» «Further moderation is expected during the northern hemisphere summer period»

The update was dated «6 June 2026», which fixes the first row below.

- 6 June 2026: the Xeneta update expected pricing pressure to begin to ease in June as capacity returns (window passed)
- northern hemisphere summer: further moderation was expected as passenger aircraft capacity returns (window passed)

*Analytical inference:* the two statements differ on timing, and the captured pages give no date for either.

## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes

The sources do not state how these rates reach a forwarder's invoice; the rate provider's analyst, as reported by StatTimes, describes ocean frontloading that could seep into airfreight: «On the ocean side, we see some frontloading. In many cases, the shippers doing this are acting now because they expect energy to become more costly, so they are producing now in anticipation of higher costs later, as well as to avoid traditional peak season surges in rates. But they then must move and sell their goods, and this is at a time of higher transportation costs. So, what happens? Demand rises and rates go up. It’s self-inflicted on the ocean side, but the longer the current market operating conditions continue, the more we could see this seep over into the airfreight»

One vendor offers a mode shift: «Sea-Air Express can deliver cargo from Asia to Europe in as few as 27 days, at rates up to 41% below pure air freight.»

*Industry interpretation:* the Sea-Air Express figures are a vendor's marketing claim about its own product, cited for navigation and not as a market rate. *Operational implication:* where a client's lane runs through the Gulf or the Red Sea, the air spot level and the sea-air alternative both belong in the quote comparison; the sources give no rate for any single lane and the corridor identity is open, since no port pair is named. The effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by these sources.

## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now

COST ALERT: the action now is to re-base open air quotes on a dated benchmark and to price the sea-air alternative next to them for Gulf and Red Sea exposed lanes.

- A pricing lead in the air freight desk refreshes, at the next quote run, the rate basis of every open air quote from a dated benchmark and records the basis on the quote.
- A sales lead puts the sea-air alternative next to the pure air quote on Asia to Europe requests, labelled as a vendor claim.
- A procurement lead asks air carriers in the next contract round whether extending an existing capacity contract carries a surcharge, since the source says shippers are temporarily accepting such surcharges.

*Operational implication:* each step uses figures the sources hold or no figure at all.
